title: “FORGIVE THEM” WAS NOT SOFT — IT WAS WAR: The Hidden Meaning That Confronts Your Pride and Exposes Your Heart
paragraphs: “FORGIVE THEM” WAS NOT SOFT — IT WAS WAR: The Hidden Meaning That Confronts Your Pride and Exposes Your Heart
There is a moment on the cross that most people read too quickly.
It’s not loud. It doesn’t shake the earth like the veil tearing. It doesn’t draw the same attention as “It is finished.”
But if you slow down… if you really sit inside it… it will confront something in you that you’ve been protecting.
Jesus, bleeding, suffocating, mocked, abandoned, betrayed…
And then He says it.
“Father, forgive them…”

In the original Greek, it’s written:
“Πάτερ, ἄφες αὐτοῖς· οὐ γὰρ οἴδασιν τί ποιοῦσιν.” (Pater, aphes autois; ou gar oidasin ti poiousin.) — Luke 23:34
“Aphes.” Forgive.
But this word isn’t passive. It isn’t gentle in the way we imagine forgiveness to be.
It comes from aphiēmi — which means to release, to send away, to let go of a debt, to cancel what is owed.
Not pretend it didn’t happen.
Not excuse it.
Cancel it.
Erase the claim.
Let it go even when justice feels deserved.
And that’s where it starts to hurt.
Because most of us don’t struggle with the idea of forgiveness…
We struggle with giving up our right to hold someone accountable in the way we think they deserve.
We want healing, but we also want them to feel what they did.
We want peace, but we still replay the offense like a courtroom in our mind.
We say we’ve “moved on”… but we haven’t released.
And Jesus, in the middle of the worst injustice in human history, didn’t just model forgiveness…
He chose it when it cost Him everything.
This wasn’t theory.
This was blood-soaked obedience.
And what makes it even more unsettling is this:
He wasn’t forgiving people who said sorry.
They weren’t repenting.
They weren’t even aware.
“οὐ γὰρ οἴδασιν” — “for they do not know.”
Not ignorance as an excuse…
But blindness as a condition.
They were spiritually blind, acting out evil they didn’t fully comprehend.
And Jesus responds not with condemnation…
But intercession.
He speaks to the Father for them.
Pause there.
Because if we’re honest, some of us aren’t even praying for the people who hurt us.
We’re replaying what they did.
We’re building silent arguments.
We’re holding emotional evidence.
But Jesus?
He becomes their advocate while they’re still harming Him.
That’s not normal.
That’s divine.
And it reveals something uncomfortable:
Forgiveness is not about the other person being worthy.
It’s about you being free.
But pride hates that.
Pride whispers, “If you forgive, you’re letting them win.”
Pride says, “They don’t deserve it.”
Pride keeps the wound open because it feels like justice.
But Scripture dismantles that thinking.

In Hebrew, forgiveness is often tied to the word:
“סָלַח” (salach) — to pardon, to spare, to release from consequence.
It’s something only God fully embodies.
And yet… He calls us into it.
Not because it’s easy.
But because it’s necessary for transformation.
Because unforgiveness doesn’t punish them…
It imprisons you.
And here’s the deeper layer most people miss:
When Jesus said “forgive them,” He wasn’t just speaking about them.
He was speaking over you.
Because at some point in your life…
You were the one who didn’t know what you were doing.
You were the one blind.
The one rebelling.
The one choosing sin over surrender.
And still…
He said “aphiēmi” over your life.
He canceled your debt.
The cross is not just where forgiveness was demonstrated.
It’s where it was paid for.
Fully.
Completely.
Without negotiation.
That’s why this message is so confronting.
Because we love receiving grace…
But we hesitate extending it.
We celebrate being forgiven…
But resist forgiving.
And somewhere in that tension, pride quietly builds a throne in our hearts.
But Jesus didn’t die so pride could stay alive.
He died to break it.
To humble us.
To remind us that we are not the judge.
We are the forgiven.
So the real question isn’t “Do they deserve forgiveness?”
The real question is…
Are you willing to look like Christ when it costs you something?
Because real forgiveness will cost you your ego.
Your right to revenge.
Your need to be right.
Your desire to see them pay.
But what you gain…
Is freedom.
Peace that isn’t dependent on apology.
Healing that doesn’t wait for closure.
And a heart that starts to look like Jesus.
Be honest.
There’s someone that came to your mind while reading this.
Someone you’ve been holding in that quiet place.
Someone whose name still stings.
This isn’t random.
This is invitation.
Not to excuse what happened…
But to release what’s been controlling you.
Sit in it.
Let it search you.
Because healing starts where honesty begins.
And if you want to go deeper…
If you’re serious about growing in Christ, healing what’s hidden, and walking in truth instead of cycles…
Not for hype.
But for transformation.
If this message reached you, don’t keep it to yourself.
If it challenged you, don’t ignore it.
If it exposed something… don’t bury it again.
Step into it.
Grow through it.
Let Jesus rewrite what pain tried to define.
Because following Christ isn’t about comfort…
It’s about transformation.
And transformation begins where pride ends.
Some wounds stay open because pride refuses to let grace touch them.
